readerTitle: Same sales, same profit. Then sales drop 20%.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (두 식당, 소프트웨어 스타트업) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 이익이 얼마나 출렁일지는 매출보다 비용 구조, 즉 고정비 비중이 정한다. 그리고 그 비중은 사업자가 고를 수 있다.
misconception: 매출이 20% 줄면 이익도 20% 정도 준다. 매출과 이익이 같은 두 사업은 위험도 같다.

sources.text: 관리회계의 표준 개념 (영업 레버리지, 고정비·변동비 구분, 공헌이익)

cards.title: Same sales, same profit. Then sales drop 20%.
body: Two restaurants each take in $100,000 a month and keep $10,000 in profit.
Restaurant A cooks in a shared kitchen rented by the hour and pays staff by the shift. Restaurant B has a big dining room on a long lease and a salaried team.
On paper they look identical. One bad season shows they are not.

image.label: Two restaurants side by side with equal profit stacks
image.brief: 두 식당을 나란히 배치. 왼쪽은 작은 공유 주방과 시간제 직원(시계 아이콘), 오른쪽은 넓은 홀과 정장 차림 직원들, 벽에 큰 임대 계약서. 각 식당 앞에 같은 높이의 동전 더미 "$10,000". 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What happens to Restaurant B's profit?
body: Restaurant B spends $60,000 a month on rent and salaries, no matter how busy it is. Food, drinks and card fees take another 30% of sales.
A slow season cuts sales 20%, from $100,000 to $80,000. What is B's profit now?

options.feedback: It feels natural, but rent and salaries don't shrink when guests stay home. The whole drop lands on profit.

options.text: About $4,000. Profit falls more than sales
options.feedback: Right direction, and that is exactly what happens to Restaurant A. B gets hit harder.
Yes. A 20% drop in sales turns a $10,000 profit into a $4,000 loss. The next card shows why.

cards.title: Same change in sales. Very different results.
body: Each lost $100 of sales costs A only $30 of profit, because A also saves $70 on food and shift wages. B saves just $30, so it loses $70. On $20,000 of lost sales, that's $6,000 for A and $14,000 for B.

cards.title: Operating leverage
body: **Operating leverage** describes how strongly profit swings when sales change. The more of your costs are fixed, the bigger the swing, both down and up.

A quick way to measure it: divide what's left after the costs that come with each sale by your profit. For B, that's $70,000 ÷ $10,000 = **7**. Each 1% change in sales moves profit about 7%. For A, the multiplier is 3.

image.label: A lever: small push on sales, big swing on profit
image.brief: 시소형 지렛대 그림. 짧은 쪽에 "Sales ±20%" 작은 화살표, 긴 쪽에 "Profit ±140%" 큰 화살표. 받침점에 "Fixed costs" 라벨. 받침점이 긴 쪽에서 멀수록 흔들림이 커지는 느낌.

cards.title: You choose your leverage.
body: Operating leverage isn't a fact of your industry. It comes from choices: buy the oven or rent it, hire salaried staff or pay by the shift, sign a long lease or take a short one.
Airlines, hotels and factories usually run high leverage. Big costs come first, and each extra guest or unit is cheap. Consultants and caterers who pay per job usually run low.
Neither is better. High leverage pays off when sales grow. Low leverage survives when they fall.
cards.softwareNote: Software often has very high operating leverage. Building the product is a big fixed cost, while serving one more user costs little. That's why growing software firms can see profit jump, and shrinking ones can see it vanish fast.

cards.title: The multiplier moves, and leverage needs cash.
body: The multiplier isn't constant. It's largest near break-even, the point where profit is zero. After B's sales rise 20%, its multiplier falls from 7 to 3.5. Swings feel most violent when profit is thin.
High fixed costs also need a cash cushion. Rent is due in the bad month too.
And going variable has a price. Renting by the hour usually costs more per unit than owning, so low leverage gives up some upside.

cards.title: Now it's a software startup.
body: Your app has grown fast, but usage jumps around week to week. Your cloud provider offers a three-year committed contract. It's much cheaper per unit than paying as you go, but you pay the full amount even if users leave.

options.text: Sign the three-year contract now to lock in the lower price
options.feedback: If growth continues, profit climbs fast. If usage drops, you're stuck with a fixed bill that eats your margin, just like Restaurant B's lease.

options.text: Pay as you go for now, then commit only to the usage you're sure of
options.feedback: You keep costs flexible while demand is unpredictable, then take the savings on a steady base. You add leverage only where sales are reliable.

options.text: Stay on pay-as-you-go permanently to stay safe
options.feedback: Safe in a downturn, but once usage is steady you pay extra for flexibility you don't need.

cards.title: Fixed costs turn small changes in sales into big changes in profit.
body: Before signing a lease, a salary or a long contract, ask how steady your sales are. Add fixed costs where demand is reliable, and keep them variable where it isn't.
**Try it today:** mark each of your costs as fixed or variable. Then work out what your profit would be if sales fell 10% next month.
